import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from itables import init_notebook_mode, show

import itables.options as opt

opt.classes="display nowrap compact"
opt.buttons=["copyHtml5", "csvHtml5", "excelHtml5"]

from cdapython import *

# CDA Madlibs

A fill in the blank notebook for `cdapython` functions, from the most basic to some of the newer/more advanced ones. Good for learning syntax and finding errors in your own code. Replace any `____#____` with your search term and the code should run. Be sure to leave quotes and stars around words that look like `"*____#____*"` or `"____#____"` and to not add quotes for `____#____`. Text after a ## in a code block is a comment explaining what the blank should be filled with, just like a madlib.
## Finding Terms to search

# Tells you what tables exist, not what is in them, just their names

tables()

# Tells you what columns exist, what table they are in, and lots of information about what is in each one

columns()

# Tells you what columns exist that have your keyword in their name, what table they are in, and lots of information about what is in each one

columns(column = "*____1____*") 

## 1) word you want to search the column name for

# Tells you what columns exist that have your keyword in their description, what table they are in, and lots of information about what is in each one


columns(description = "*____1____*") 

## 1) word you want to search the description for

# Gives you a list of what values are in a column of your choice, and how many times each value appears

column_values( "____1____" )

## 1) column name you want to see the possible values for

# Same as above, but restricted to a single upstream data source -- useful if you only care what values show up
# at one particular data center. Valid data_source values are 'GDC', 'PDC', 'IDC', 'GC', 'ICDC', and 'CTDC'.
# Unlike every other function in this notebook, column_values() only accepts ONE data_source at a time, not a list.

column_values( "____1____", data_source = "____2____" )

## 1) column name you want to see the possible values for
## 2) the single data source you want to restrict to, e.g. GDC

## Searching without knowing a column name at all

Every function below that starts with `summarize_` or `get_` also accepts one or more bare search terms with no column name attached, searched across every column at once. This is the fastest way to get a first answer to "is there any data about X" before you've looked up any column names.

# Searches every column at once for your word, and gives you back a summary

summarize_subjects('____1____')

## 1) a plain word or phrase to search for, e.g. 'kidney'

# Adding a second word means "must touch both" -- every result below is connected to BOTH words somewhere in its record

summarize_subjects('____1____', '____2____')

## 1) first plain word or phrase to search for
## 2) second plain word or phrase you ALSO want every result to touch
## Looking at data

# Gives you a readout of the columns for the subject table, what values exist in each column, and how many times each value occurs AFTER filtering the data by some filter you set

summarize_subjects(match_all=['____1____ = ____2____'])

## 1) column name you want to filter
## 2) column value you want to filter by

# Gives you a readout of the columns for the file table, what values exist in each column, and how many times each value occurs AFTER filtering the data by multiple filters you set
# This will return only data that has BOTH the conditions of ##2/##3 and ##4/##5


summarize_files(match_all=['____1____ = ____2____', '____3____ = ____4____'])

## 1) first column name you want to filter
## 2) first column value you want to filter by
## 3) second column name you ALSO want to filter
## 4) second column value you ALSO want to filter by


#You can add as many comma seperated pairs like ##1 and ##2 as you like

# Gives you a readout of the columns for your chosen table, what values exist in each column, and how many times each value occurs AFTER filtering the data by multiple filters you set
# This will return ALL data that has EITHER of the conditions of ##2/##3 and ##4/##5

summarize_subjects( match_any=['____1____ = ____2____', '____3____ = ____4____'])

## 1) first column name you want to filter
## 2) first column value you want to filter by
## 3) second column name you want to filter
## 4) second column value you want to filter by


#You can add as many comma seperated pairs like ##1 and ##2 as you like

# This works just like summarize_subjects or summarize_files, but instead of giving you a summary, it gives you a big matrix of all the data. 
# Gives you a matrix of all the columns for your table and one row per value AFTER filtering the data by multiple filters you set
# This will return only data that has the conditions of ##1/##2

get_file_data(match_all=['____1____ = ____2____'])

## 1) column name you want to filter
## 2) column value you want to filter by

# This works just like summarize_subjects or summarize_files, but instead of giving you a summary, it gives you a big matrix of all the data. 
# Gives you a matrix of all the columns for your table and one row per value AFTER filtering the data by multiple filters you set
# This will return only data that has BOTH the conditions of ##1/##2 and ##3/##4


get_subject_data( match_all=['____1____ = ____2____', '____4____ = ____5____'])

## 1) first column name you want to filter
## 2) first column value you want to filter by
## 3) second column name you ALSO want to filter
## 4) second column value you ALSO want to filter by


#You can add as many comma seperated pairs like ##1 and ##2 as you like

# This works just like summarize_subjects or summarize_files, but instead of giving you a summary, it gives you a big matrix of all the data. 
# Gives you a matrix of all the columns for your chosen table and one row per value AFTER filtering the data by multiple filters you set
# This will return ALL data that has EITHER of the conditions of ##1/##2 and ##3/##4

get_file_data(match_any=['____1____ = ____2____', '____3____ = ____4____'])

## 1) first column name you want to filter
## 2) first column value you want to filter by
## 3) second column name you want to filter
## 4) second column value you want to filter by


#You can add as many comma seperated pairs like ##1 and ##2 as you like

# For more complicated questions, you can have both a match_all and a match_any. 
# It will return all the data that has both all the conditions in your match_all, and at least one of the condtions in your match_any

get_subject_data( match_all=['____1____ = ____2____', '____3____ = ____4____'], match_any=['____5____ = ____6____', '____7____ = ____8____'])

## 1) first column name you want to filter
## 2) first column value you want to filter by
## 3) second column name you want to filter
## 4) second column value you want to filter by
## 5) third column name you want to filter
## 6) third column value you want to filter by
## 7) fourth column name you want to filter
## 8) fourth column value you want to filter by

# Restrict any search to one or more specific upstream data sources. Unlike column_values(), this DOES accept a list.
# Valid values are 'GDC', 'PDC', 'IDC', 'GC', 'ICDC', and 'CTDC'.

get_subject_data( match_all=['____1____ = ____2____'], data_source = ['____3____'])

## 1) column name you want to filter
## 2) column value you want to filter by
## 3) the data source(s) you want to restrict to, e.g. 'GDC' -- or a list like ['GDC', 'IDC']
## Pulling in extra columns

# add_columns pulls in columns from a second table into your results.
# A single column name adds just that column; a table name followed by .* (e.g. 'file.*') adds every column from that table.

get_subject_data( match_all=['____1____ = ____2____'], add_columns = '____3____')

## 1) column name you want to filter
## 2) column value you want to filter by
## 3) the column (or table.*) you want added, e.g. 'file.*'

# collate_results=True pairs up all the related values from an added table (like file.* above) so that values
# that actually belong to the same row stay together, instead of being mashed into separate lists.
# This also works with summarize_subjects() and summarize_files().

get_subject_data( match_all=['____1____ = ____2____'], add_columns = '____3____', collate_results = True)

## 1) column name you want to filter
## 2) column value you want to filter by
## 3) the column (or table.*) you want added, e.g. 'file.*'

# When collate_results=True has given you a nested column, expand_subject_results() (or expand_file_results()
# for file-based searches) flattens it into a plain table, with one row per nested value instead of one row per subject.

my_results = get_subject_data( match_all=['____1____ = ____2____'], add_columns = '____3____', collate_results = True)
expand_subject_results(my_results, '____4____')

## 1) column name you want to filter
## 2) column value you want to filter by
## 3) the column (or table.*) you want added, e.g. 'file.*'
## 4) the name of the new nested column to flatten, e.g. 'file_data'
## Seeing why a harmonized value matched

# add_extras shows the real underlying vocabulary behind a harmonized match -- it doesn't change which rows match,
# it just annotates why. This is most useful on anatomic_site and disease, the two fields backed by a real ontology.
# Valid values are 'synonym_terms', 'slim_terms', 'containing_terms', or 'all'.

summarize_subjects('____1____', add_extras = ['____2____'])

## 1) a plain word or phrase to search for, e.g. 'melanoma'
## 2) which extra metadata to add, e.g. 'all'
## Searching with a list of IDs you already have

# match_from_file lets you check a TSV file of IDs you already have against CDA, instead of typing each one into a filter by hand.
# If your file has a data center's own native IDs (e.g. a GDC case UUID), match against 'upstream_id'.
# If your file has CDA's own subject IDs, match against 'subject_id' instead.

get_subject_data(
    match_from_file={
        'input_file': '____1____',
        'input_column': '____2____',
        'cda_column_to_match': '____3____'
    }
)

## 1) the name of your TSV file, e.g. 'my_cases.tsv'
## 2) the column in that file with the IDs in it
## 3) the CDA column to match against -- 'upstream_id' for native source IDs, 'subject_id' for CDA's own IDs
## Combining two separate searches

# If you need an "AND" condition across two different values of the SAME column (like two different file_types,
# where no single file can have both), match_all can't do it in one call -- run two separate searches and
# intersect them instead. intersect_file_results() works the same way for file-based searches.

first_group = get_subject_data(match_all=['____1____ = ____2____'])
second_group = get_subject_data(match_all=['____1____ = ____3____'])
intersect_subject_results(first_group, second_group)

## 1) the column both searches share, e.g. 'file_type'
## 2) the value for the first group, e.g. 'CT Image Storage'
## 3) the value for the second group, e.g. 'Annotated Somatic Mutation'
